h1: Getting beer label approval from the excise department
title: Beer Label Approval From Excise | Craft Beer School
desc: How label approval from a state excise department usually works: what to prepare, the order of steps and the mistakes that cause rejections.
teaser: A label you have printed is a label you may have to pull. Get the approval order right and the excise office stops being the bottleneck.
standfirst: Alcohol is a state subject in India, so every state decides how a beer label gets approved. The pattern is similar everywhere. Here is the order to work in and what to have in your hand before you apply.
sections:
Most states want a beer label registered with the excise department before the beer can be sold under it. Some also ask for the brand name itself to be registered. Printing first is the expensive mistake. A reel of 50,000 can labels or a shrink sleeve run is paid for before anyone has told you that the brand name is too close to an existing one.

Rules, forms, fees and timelines differ by state and they change. Treat this guide as a map of the process. For the real requirements, read the current notification from your state excise department or work with a licensing adviser. Our guide on the microbrewery licence in India shows where label approval sits in the wider licensing sequence.
Know what the label must carry

Before you design anything, list the mandatory statements. They usually come from three places: the state excise rules, the central food safety labelling rules and the packaged goods rules that govern how a net quantity is declared. Typical items are the brand name, the type of product, the alcohol by volume, the net volume, the name and address of the manufacturer, a batch or date marking and the statutory health warning.

Some states add their own lines. A few restrict certain words or imagery. The one thing every state shares is that the label cannot mislead. Our guide on what a beer label must show covers the content in detail. Beer label rules in India covers how the rules vary.
Bring a dossier, not just a design

Excise officers read applications, not artwork. A clean file helps. Prepare the following before you submit:

  • Artwork as it will print, at actual size, with every mandatory statement visible.
  • The brand name and any trademark search or filing you have made.
  • A product description: style, ingredients and the declared strength.
  • Your licence details and the plant address exactly as they appear on the licence.
  • Any laboratory report the state asks for to support the declared strength.

Keep one folder, paper and digital, with the date each item went in. When an officer asks a question six weeks later, the folder answers it.
Declare a strength you can defend

The alcohol figure is the line most likely to come back to you later. Estimate it from your own gravity readings using ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25. A beer that starts at 1.052 and finishes at 1.010 works out at about 5.5%. Then check the packaged beer with a proper instrument, because the formula is an estimate and a label is a declaration.

Choose one measuring method and use it every time, so the number on the label and the number in the lab report come from the same source. If a batch drifts, a declared 5.0% on a beer that tests at 5.6% is a compliance problem and not a typing error.

Approval is rarely instant. Applications can sit while an officer is on inspection duty, during budget periods or around the annual licence renewals. Ask the department how long a typical label takes, then add a margin. Build the label date into your launch plan next to the brewery commissioning date, not after it. Our guide on Maharashtra beer excise and licences shows how one state lays out the chain.

If you plan several beers, submit them together where the state allows it. If you plan seasonal beers, ask whether a new batch label needs fresh approval or only a changed one.
Mistakes that send a label back

• Strength on the label that does not match the strength on the application.
  • A brand name that is too close to an approved one.
  • Claims such as "smooth" or "energising" that imply a benefit or effect.
  • A warning that is too small or hard to read against a dark background.
  • An address that differs from the licence.
  • Artwork on the application that differs from the printed label.

The last one catches people out. A designer tweaks the layout after approval. The printed label is then no longer the approved label. Freeze the artwork the day you apply and change it only through the department.

Write the mandatory statements for your first label on one page. Check them against the current notification from your state. Then phone the excise office or your licensing adviser with three questions: what documents they want, how long approval takes and whether a changed batch date needs a fresh approval. You will know more after that call than from a week of reading.
faqs: Do I need excise approval before printing labels?
In most states, yes, or at least you take the risk of reprinting. Check your state's current notification. Ask the excise office before you commit to a print run.
Does every state use the same label rules?
No. Alcohol is a state subject, so approval steps, forms, fees and some wording rules differ. The central food safety and packaged goods rules sit alongside them.
Can I put a new batch date on an approved label?
It depends on the state. Some treat a date field as part of the approved design. Others want a fresh approval for any change. Ask the department before you print.
How do I find out my beer's strength for the label?
Estimate it from gravity readings using ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25, then confirm the packaged beer with an instrument or a laboratory test. Use the same method every time.
